analysis.one_liner: Forces big-money political groups to register and disclose donors, while lifting party spending caps.
analysis.headline: The House passed the 527 Reform Act 218-209 in April 2006, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: "527 organizations" are tax-exempt groups that spent unlimited money to sway federal elections without registering under federal campaign finance law. This bill would force any such group that spends more than $1,000 supporting or attacking a federal candidate to register as a political committee, disclose its donors, and obey contribution limits. At the same time, it would remove the cap on how much national party committees may spend to support their candidates and raise contribution limits for candidates running against wealthy self-funded opponents.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would be able to see who is paying for campaign ads and election-year groups; candidates facing wealthy self-funded rivals, who could raise more from small donors; and national party committees, which could spend unlimited amounts supporting their candidates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting disclosure of campaign money

how_it_helps.text: Any 527 group spending over $1,000 promoting, attacking, or opposing a federal candidate would count as a federal political committee and have to follow campaign finance disclosure and contribution rules.
Donations to the non-federal accounts of these political committees would be capped at $25,000 per person per year, closing an unlimited-donation channel.
The bill raises contribution limits for House and Senate candidates facing wealthy self-funded opponents, making it easier for their challengers to compete.
Purely state and local political groups are exempt, so grassroots groups that never touch federal races would not be burdened.

analysis.who_pays: 527 organizations and the large donors funding them, who would lose an unlimited, low-disclosure channel for influencing federal elections; political parties and their donors would gain, since party spending caps would be repealed.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the existing cap on how much national party committees can spend on behalf of candidates, allowing unlimited party spending in federal races — a significant expansion of one form of money in politics that supporters of the 527 rules had to accept as part of the package.

The new rules are complex: groups face 100% or 50% federal-funding requirements for ads and voter registration and get-out-the-vote activities, with detailed tests for what counts as a federal reference, which could chill or push away grassroots voter-drive activity by advocacy groups.

The bill carves out a special fast-track court process for constitutional challenges, but Members of Congress can sue to challenge the law themselves, inviting litigation that could stall the rules for years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: closing an unlimited, lightly disclosed spending channel in exchange for unlimited party spending through regulated channels. Voters get clearer disclosure either way, but the bill does not reduce total money in federal elections so much as move it — and the party-spending repeal is a serious cost that honest supporters would concede. The bill's heavy procedural complexity and its special court track also made its rules hard to enforce quickly.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 218-209, the Senate put it on its calendar but never voted, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Shays introduced the bill in the House on February 2, 2005, and it was referred to the Committee on House Administration.
The committee reported the bill as amended on July 22, 2005, after approving it 5-3 without a recommendation.
The House passed the bill 218-209 on April 5, 2006: 211 of 231 Republicans voted yes while 190 of 201 Democrats voted no.
The Senate received the bill on April 6, 2006, placed it on its legislative calendar, and never took it up; it died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: 527 organizations and the large donors who fund them came out ahead: with no Senate vote, they kept spending to influence federal elections without registering as federal political committees or disclosing under campaign finance law. National party committees also kept their existing spending limits rather than the unlimited spending this bill would have allowed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unregistered 527 groups and their big donors

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Introduced the 527 Reform Act and led it through the House.

against.name: Sen. Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was placed on the calendar.

against.name: Sens. John McCain and Christopher Dodd
against.role: Senators leading opposition in the Senate
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill and worked to keep it from advancing in the Senate, favoring a different 527 disclosure approach.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was sharply partisan: 211 of 231 House Republicans voted yes and only 7 of 201 Democrats did, a 218-209 margin; both parties had allied 527 groups that the bill would have regulated.

industries.industry: 527 political organizations (issue groups, ideological groups, and labor-affiliated committees)
industries.note: The bill would force these groups to register as federal political committees, disclose donors, and accept contribution limits, ending their ability to spend unlimited money on federal elections with little disclosure. Ordinary voters have an interest in knowing who funds campaign ads, which is exactly what these groups' exemption lets them avoid.

industries.industry: Large individual donors to political groups
industries.note: Donations to the non-federal accounts of these committees would be capped at $25,000 per person per year, ending a channel for giving far beyond normal campaign limits.

The bill repeals the cap on party spending on behalf of candidates, letting parties spend unlimited amounts through disclosed channels. Money would shift from lightly regulated 527s toward party committees, which operate under stricter reporting rules.
By raising contribution limits for opponents of candidates who spend their own fortunes, the bill would make it easier for challengers to compete against them.
